personality_voice.book_baseline: Ernie in the books is defined by a cluster of highly consistent, observable traits: pomposity and self-importance (puffing out his chest, speaking in loud carrying voices, holding forth on matters of import), a tendency toward dramatic moral pronouncements delivered with solemnity, genuine courage tempered by institutional anxiety about rules and status (his prefect badge dilemma), an ability to apologize sincerely and formally when wrong, intellectual enthusiasm that tips into boastfulness (his OWL revision recital), and a recurring pattern of aligning himself loudly with the right side once he has decided. His speech is formal, verbose, and portentous — he uses phrases like 'I personally believe,' 'I am at a loss to see why,' 'I must say,' 'I, personally.' He is capable of fear (trembling while confronting Harry in CoS), stubbornness (maintaining his accusation while physically shaking), and genuine warmth. He is recognizably Hufflepuff — loyal, institutionally minded, group-oriented — but complicated by his pomposity and class-consciousness (his nine generations of pure blood).
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains only the Knight Bus driver Ernie Prang from PoA, not Ernie Macmillan. The film scenes labeled in the corpus show 'Ernie' as a silent, sweating, unshaven bus driver who grunts monosyllabically ('Ar,' implied by the book scenes referenced) and reacts physically to driving rather than speaking. This is an entirely different character. Ernie Macmillan himself does not appear in any of the provided film scenes. There is no film evidence of the pompous, formal, morally declarative, institutionally anxious personality that defines book-Ernie Macmillan.
personality_voice.difference: The film corpus provides zero portrayal of Ernie Macmillan's personality and voice. The only 'Ernie' in the film corpus is Ernie Prang, a background Knight Bus driver with no dialogue attributed to Macmillan. All of Ernie Macmillan's defining traits — pomposity, formal speech, moral courage, institutional anxiety, sincerity, boastfulness, the DA hesitation, the OWL obsession, the Battle of Hogwarts stand — are absent from the film corpus entirely.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: Because the film corpus contains no portrayal of Ernie Macmillan at all (only a different character named Ernie), virtually none of the book-established personality and voice can be evaluated as preserved. However, Ernie Macmillan does appear briefly in the actual films (notably in Order of the Phoenix and Deathly Hallows), so the absence from this corpus is a corpus limitation rather than a complete film absence. Given the corpus as provided, there is almost no film evidence to score against the rich book baseline. A score of 8 reflects that the character's broad identity (Hufflepuff student, DA member) is theoretically recognizable from general film knowledge, but the corpus itself gives no evidence of his defining voice or personality traits being preserved.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Not enough evidence in film corpus; the film corpus provided does not contain Ernie Macmillan scenes.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Ernie Macmillan serves several distinct narrative functions across the books: (1) In CoS, he is the primary voice of student suspicion against Harry, functioning as an antagonist-by-misunderstanding who forces Harry to confront how he is perceived, then completes a mini-arc of apology; (2) In GoF, he is a social barometer of Harry's shifting status among peers; (3) In OotP, he is a DA co-founder with real agency — he initiates the public declaration of support for Harry, hesitates meaningfully over signing the list (creating dramatic tension), and serves as a classroom participant whose actions others watch and imitate; (4) In HBP, he is a recurring Potions partner who drives minor scene beats (asking about Felix Felicis, using 'Specialis Revelio' which Harry and Ron copy); (5) In DH, he has perhaps his most consequential moment of agency: standing up at the Hufflepuff table and shouting 'And what if we want to stay and fight?' — a call that receives applause and represents the Hufflepuff voice at the Battle of Hogwarts; he also casts a Patronus that saves Harry, Ron, and Hermione from dementors.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no scenes in which Ernie Macmillan exercises agency. His narrative functions — accusing Harry, apologizing, joining the DA, defending Harry publicly, standing up to fight, casting a Patronus — do not appear in the provided film corpus. The only 'Ernie' present is the bus driver.
narrative_role_agency.difference: All of Ernie's narrative functions and agency are absent from the film corpus. His most significant acts of agency — the CoS accusation-and-apology arc, the OotP public declaration, the DH battle cry, the Patronus — cannot be evaluated as present or absent from film evidence provided.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The corpus gives no film scenes for Ernie Macmillan specifically. Based on general knowledge of the films, Ernie Macmillan's CoS role (the accusation) was not filmed in any meaningful way; his DA participation is backgrounded; his DH battle cry and Patronus are not depicted with the same clarity or agency as in the books. The score of 6 reflects the near-total absence of his narrative agency from what the film corpus shows, with slight credit for his background presence in DA scenes in the actual films.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Not enough evidence in film corpus.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Ernie's motivations are layered and consistent: he is motivated by a desire to be on the right side morally and institutionally, by status anxiety (his prefect badge, his pure-blood lineage as a defensive credential), by genuine loyalty to Dumbledore and Hogwarts, and by a need to be seen as a serious, important participant in events. His internal conflict in OotP — wanting to fight Umbridge's regime but being genuinely worried about the consequences for his prefect status — is directly evidenced in dialogue ('We are prefects... if this list was found'). He resolves this conflict by signing. His CoS motivation (self-protective fear leading to scapegoating, then guilt leading to apology) is also clearly traced.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: No film scenes show Ernie Macmillan's motivations. The corpus provides nothing from which to evaluate whether his status anxiety, institutional loyalty, or moral courage are conveyed.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: All motivational texture is absent from the film corpus. The conflict between his rule-following instincts and his moral convictions — the most interesting thing about him motivationally — does not appear.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: With no film corpus evidence, it is impossible to confirm any motivational preservation. A score of 5 reflects that his broad motivation (support for the right side) may be implied by his background DA presence in the actual films, but his specific internal conflicts are almost certainly lost.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Not enough evidence in film corpus.

character_arc.book_baseline: Ernie has a clear micro-arc within CoS: begins as the loudest voice accusing Harry, maintains his position stubbornly even when confronted, then formally and sincerely apologizes once Hermione is attacked, extending his hand. This is a small but complete arc — accusation, confrontation, resolution, reconciliation. Across the series, he also has a broader arc from institutional rule-follower to someone willing to defy authority (signing the DA list despite prefect status, standing up at the Battle of Hogwarts). The CoS arc is the most fully realized.
character_arc.film_portrayal: No arc is visible in the film corpus. The CoS accusation-and-apology arc, which is the clearest character arc Ernie has, does not appear in the provided film scenes. His broader growth arc is also unrepresented.
character_arc.difference: The CoS arc is essentially unfilmed in any meaningful way in the actual movies, reducing a complete small arc to nothing. His broader arc from cautious institutionalist to battle participant is compressed to invisibility.
character_arc.penalty_logic: A score of 3 reflects that the most defining arc the character has is absent or non-functional in the films. The DH moment ('And what if we want to stay and fight?') may exist in some form in the actual film, but it lacks the context built across earlier books to register as an arc payoff.
character_arc.evidence_status: Not enough evidence in film corpus.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Ernie's key relationships are: (1) Harry — an adversarial-to-respectful dynamic, starting with accusation and ending in genuine mutual regard ('Harry liked him despite his pompous manner'); (2) Hannah Abbott — his consistent companion and audience, a warm friendship; (3) The DA group collectively — Ernie as a committed, slightly self-important member who nonetheless performs; (4) Justin Finch-Fletchley — his close Hufflepuff ally. The Harry-Ernie dynamic is the most dramatically important: it moves from public antagonism to qualified friendship over six books.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: No relationship dynamics involving Ernie Macmillan appear in the film corpus. The Harry-Ernie dynamic — which requires the CoS scenes to exist at all — has no foundation in the films as presented in this corpus.
key_relationships.difference: The Harry-Ernie dynamic, which is the most important relationship Ernie has, is largely absent from the films because the CoS accusation-apology arc was not meaningfully depicted. Without that foundation, their later mutual respect has no dramatic weight.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: A score of 3 reflects that while Ernie appears alongside Harry and other DA members in the actual films, the emotional dynamic of earned respect replacing initial antagonism is absent, and Hannah Abbott's consistent companionship is not developed.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Not enough evidence in film corpus.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Ernie is a genuinely complex minor character. His complexity comes from the tension between his pomposity and his genuine courage; his ability to be simultaneously self-important and sincerely correct; his class-consciousness (pure-blood defense in CoS) coexisting with his eventual full commitment to the anti-Voldemort cause; his DA hesitation revealing real institutional anxiety rather than cowardice; his OWL revision boasting revealing insecurity beneath the confident surface; his Battle of Hogwarts cry being both dramatic and completely in character. He is funny precisely because he is earnest. He is admirable precisely because he overcomes his own pomposity to do the right thing.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: None of this complexity is present in the film corpus. The pomposity-courage tension, the class-consciousness, the DA hesitation, the OWL anxiety, the CoS apology — all absent. Ernie in the films is a background figure whose texture is almost entirely lost.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The gap between book-Ernie and film-Ernie is the difference between a fully realized minor character with consistent, observable contradictions and a near-invisible background extra. The most nuanced material — his CoS scenes, his OotP hesitation, his DH stand — is either absent or reduced to a moment without context.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: A score of 4 reflects near-total loss of complexity. The character remains nominally present (a recognizable name, a Hufflepuff, a DA member) but the material that makes him interesting — his contradictions, his arc, his voice — is absent from the film corpus and largely absent from the actual films.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Not enough evidence in film corpus; reasonably inferred from general film knowledge that most book nuance is lost.

comparative.key_observations: The film corpus provided contains no scenes featuring Ernie Macmillan — only scenes featuring the entirely distinct character Ernie Prang (Knight Bus driver). Ernie Macmillan's film portrayal, based on the corpus and general knowledge of the films, is a near-complete reduction of a richly textured minor character to a background extra. Every defining element of his book characterization — his pomposity-courage contradiction, his CoS accusation-and-apology arc, his OotP DA hesitation, his DH battle cry and Patronus — is either absent from the films or reduced to a fleeting moment without the contextual scaffolding that gives it meaning. He is one of the books' most successfully realized minor characters precisely because his traits are consistent, funny, and dramatically useful across all seven books; the films lose almost all of this. The score of 29 reflects that a name and a house affiliation remain, but the character does not.
